Dermatology · published research

Androgenetic alopecia

Sham-controlled studies report short-term increases in hair density with some devices. Evidence does not establish lasting benefit after treatment stops or superiority to minoxidil.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Sham-controlled studies report short-term increases in hair density with some devices. Evidence does not establish lasting benefit after treatment stops or superiority to minoxidil.

Summary of the Evidence

The androgenetic alopecia category contains 95 publications, including 40 human primary reports, two in-vitro studies, and many reviews, meta-analyses, protocols, surveys, and commentary. One publication reports four separate randomized trials and another contains two studies; reviews reuse those and other primary cohorts. The 95 publications should therefore not be read as 95 independent clinical trials. Several studies test devices alongside other care.

Human and clinical evidence

Multiple sham-controlled trials report increased hair density or terminal-hair counts during treatment. In a 40-person trial, a helmet device using visible red wavelengths of 630, 650, and 660 nm was worn for 18 minutes daily over 24 weeks. Hair density and diameter measures increased versus sham, while the patient global assessment did not significantly differ (Kim et al. 2013). In a 2025 randomized comparison involving 91 men, both low-level light and 5% topical minoxidil groups improved from their own starting measurements, but the study did not find a significant between-group difference (Neema et al. 2025). This does not establish that the treatments are equivalent. Other trials vary in device, blinding, follow-up, and whether treatment is used alone or as an add-on.

Animal evidence

No animal study is listed in this indication category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Two laboratory studies use human follicular or dermal-papilla cells. They report changes in cell proliferation, migration, or signaling under selected exposures. These cell findings help define possible mechanisms but do not show how much hair a person will grow.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Most clinical devices deliver visible red light around 630–660 nm; some use near-infrared wavelengths near 785 nm. Helmets, caps, and combs are used for daily or alternate-day sessions over roughly four to six months. Fluence and irradiance reporting is uneven, and some designs test multiple wavelengths together. The studies do not identify a single optimal dose, a durable effect after stopping, or reliable superiority over established drug therapy.

Interpretation

The repeated sham-controlled observations support short-term hair-density improvement with some devices during continued use. They do not show that every device produces the same effect, that gains persist after use stops, or that light outperforms minoxidil. Reviews add context but not new participant cohorts.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term hair-density improvement during treatment Low for durability after stopping treatment or superiority to minoxidil
Publications and records95 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several sham-controlled studies report increased hair density during treatment, supporting a low-to-moderate rating for that measured outcome. However, devices and protocols differ, reviews repeat the same trials, and some studies have substantial attrition. Active comparisons have not established superiority to minoxidil. Larger independent trials with post-treatment follow-up would clarify size and durability of benefit.
